sections.title: Preface

summary.text: The preface explains that the Immunological Basis for Immunization series began in 1993 with eight modules on the vaccines of the Expanded Programme on Immunization and has been widely used. It notes that the series is being updated and extended with new modules, including this one on mumps.

sections.extract: This module is part of the series The Immunological Basis for Immunization, which was initially developed in 1993 as a set of eight modules focusing on the vaccines included in the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI)1. In addition to a general immunology module, each of the seven other modules covered one of the vaccines recommended as part of the EPI programme, i.e. diphtheria, measles, pertussis, polio,

sections.title: Mumps disease

summary.text: Describes mumps as an acute viral illness marked by swelling of the parotid or other salivary glands, spread by contact with respiratory droplets or saliva and less infectious than measles or varicella. It explains how the virus replicates and spreads in the body and the timing of infectiousness. It lists complications such as orchitis, meningitis, encephalitis and deafness, with their frequencies.

sections.extract: Mumps disease Mumps is an acute viral illness characterized by unilateral or bilateral tenderness or swelling of the parotid or other salivary glands. Mumps is transmitted through person-to-person contact or by direct contact with respiratory droplets or saliva from an infected person. By comparison to measles and varicella, which can be transmitted by aerosol spread, mumps is less infectious (Hope-Simpson, 1952).

sections.title: Mumps virus

summary.text: Describes the mumps virus as an enveloped, negative-sense RNA virus in the Paramyxoviridae family, with its size, genome and the proteins encoded by its genes. It notes the roles of the structural and nonstructural proteins and the genotyping scheme.

sections.extract: Mumps virus Mumps virus is a single-stranded, negative sense, enveloped ribonucleic acid (RNA) virus in the Paramyxoviridae family, Paramyxovirinae sub-family, genus Rubulavirus. Mumps virions are pleomorphic but generally spherical structures, and range in size from 85 nm to 300 nm in diameter (Cantell, 1961). The viral genome is 15 384 nucleotides in length and encodes nine proteins from seven genes. The mumps

sections.title: Mumps vaccines

summary.text: Reviews mumps vaccines from the first inactivated vaccine of 1946, discontinued because immunity was short-lived, to the many live attenuated strains used since. It describes strains such as Jeryl Lynn, Urabe, Leningrad-3 and others, including how they were developed. A table compares reported rates of aseptic meningitis after vaccination with different strains in various countries.

sections.extract: Mumps vaccines The first mumps vaccine was developed in 1946 (Habel, 1946). It was based on formalin- inactivated virus, but was discontinued because immunity was short-lived (Habel, 1951). Since then numerous mumps vaccine strains have been developed and used in vaccines throughout the world. sections.title: Immunological response to natural infection

summary.text: Notes that immunity after natural mumps infection probably involves both antibodies and cellular immunity, that no definitive correlates of protection exist, and that research is limited compared with measles and rubella.

sections.extract: The immune response to mumps virus infection is likely to be the result of a complex interplay between both the humoral and cellular arms of the immune response, and no definitive correlates of protection have yet been identified. Studies on the immune response to mumps infection are quite limited in comparison to those described for measles and rubella infections.

sections.title: Antibody response to mumps infection in unvaccinated individuals

summary.text: Describes the antibody response to mumps in unvaccinated people, with IgM appearing within days of symptoms and peaking around one week. IgG rises to a peak in about three weeks and persists, while salivary IgA can be detected for several weeks.

sections.extract: Antibody response to mumps infection in unvaccinated individuals In naive individuals immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies are measurable within a few days of symptom onset. IgM peaks about one week after the onset of parotitis or symptoms, and is detectable for weeks to months after parotitis onset (Ukkonen et al., 1981; Benito et al., 1987). Low avidity IgG may also be present at the time of symptom onset, although

sections.title: Cell-mediated immunity following natural mumps disease

summary.text: Describes cell-mediated immunity after natural mumps, noting that lymphocytes are thought to aid recovery but that little is known about mumps-specific cellular immunity. It cites studies linking cytotoxic and proliferative lymphocyte responses with infection.

sections.extract: Cell-mediated immunity following natural mumps disease Lymphocytes are known to play an important role in host response to viral infections, and are believed to have a significant function in the immune response to mumps and recovery from mumps infection. sections.title: Maternal antibody

summary.text: Explains that maternal antibodies to mumps cross the placenta and likely protect infants, citing lower mumps rates in infants under one year. It reports studies on how long maternal antibodies remain detectable during the first year.

sections.extract: Maternal antibody Maternal antibody (IgG) to mumps following natural infection is transferred across the placenta and is believed to provide protection to infants against clinical mumps. Clinical mumps occurs less frequently in infants aged less than one year (12% to 17%) compared to children aged one to four years (68%) (Philip et al., 1959; Meyer, 1962; Reed et al., 1967). sections.title: Duration of immunity to natural mumps infection

summary.text: Explains that natural mumps infection is generally thought to give long-lasting immunity, though confirmed reinfections have been reported and may be more common than believed.

sections.extract: Duration of immunity to natural mumps infection Natural mumps virus infection is generally believed to provide long-lasting immunity. Twenty or more years after their mumps illness, most (82%) individuals still had detectable haemagglutination-inhibiting antibodies (Levitt et al., 1970). However, cases of clinically apparent mumps reinfection that have been confirmed with epidemiological links or laboratory tests

sections.title: Antibody response following vaccination

summary.text: Reports that over 90% of children develop mumps antibodies after vaccination, with similar seroconversion across major vaccine strains, and discusses responses to one and two doses. A table summarizes seroconversion studies. It notes that revaccination raised antibody titres in more than half of recipients and reduced the share with low titres.

sections.extract: Antibody response following vaccination In general, over 90% of infants and children develop detectable antibodies against mumps following vaccination with mumps vaccines (Table 2). Seroconversion rates are comparable for vaccine combinations with Jeryl Lynn, RIT 4385 and Urabe Am 9 strains (Isomura et al., 1973; Vesikari et al., 1983b; Usonis et al., 1998; Usonis et al., 1999; Usonis et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2002)

sections.title: Cell-mediated immunity following mumps vaccination

summary.text: Reports that most vaccinated children with mumps antibodies also show lymphocyte responses, that cellular responses are similar across ages regardless of maternal antibody, and that HLA associations suggest genetic influence on the immune response.

sections.extract: Cell-mediated immunity following mumps vaccination Following vaccination with live attenuated mumps vaccine, most, but not all children with anti-mumps antibody in their sera, demonstrated a lymphocyte proliferative response to mumps antigen (Ilonen, 1979; Ilonen et al., 1984). sections.title: Duration of immunity to mumps vaccination

summary.text: Notes that data on long-term immunity after mumps vaccination are limited, though antibodies persist in most people about ten years after one MMR dose, with variation by laboratory method. It discusses waning antibody levels after two doses. It ends by listing open questions on cellular immunity and boosting from exposure to wild virus.

sections.extract: Duration of immunity to mumps vaccination Data regarding long-term immunity against mumps after vaccination are limited. Studies indicate that one dose of MMR vaccine can provide persistent antibodies to mumps. sections.title: Correlates of immunity

summary.text: Discusses correlates of immunity to mumps, explaining that neutralizing antibodies seem a reasonable marker though no serological test reliably predicts protection. It calls for more research, including on cell-mediated immunity markers.

sections.extract: Correlates of immunity Humoral immunity is important in protection against mumps, and antibody measurements are often used as a surrogate measure of immunity to viral infections. However, there is poor correlation between assays that measure neutralization and less labour-intensive methods that measure the presence of mumps antibody (Pipkin et al., 1999). sections.title: Laboratory diagnosis of mumps

summary.text: Notes that mumps is often diagnosed clinically from parotitis but that laboratory confirmation may be needed because other causes exist and mumps is becoming rare.

sections.extract: 14 A clinical diagnosis of mumps is frequently made when parotitis is evident at the time of patient examination. However, since parotitis may be caused by other viral or non- viral diseases or conditions, laboratory confirmation using virological or serological techniques may be needed, especially as mumps disease becomes rare due to increased vaccination.

sections.title: Virological methods

summary.text: Describes virological methods for diagnosing mumps, including virus stability in storage, specimen types and timing of collection. It notes that RNA detection by RT-PCR is generally more sensitive than culture.

sections.extract: Virological methods Mumps virus is stable for several days at 4°C. Stability increases with decreasing temperature and the virus can be stored indefinitely at -70°C. Specimen quality appears to greatly impact the ability to culture mumps virus and detect mumps RNA using reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) (Utz et al., 1958). sections.title: Serological methods

summary.text: Describes serological diagnosis of mumps, explaining that IgM detection works well in unvaccinated patients if specimens are well timed but may fail in vaccinated people with a secondary immune response. A table sets out expected laboratory results by vaccination status and timing of collection.

sections.extract: Serological methods Detection of mumps-specific IgM antibody in serum or saliva is a good diagnostic measure in unvaccinated patients. Timing of specimen collection is important to consider in interpreting laboratory results. sections.title: Diagnostic challenges

summary.text: Explains that laboratory diagnosis of mumps is difficult in highly vaccinated populations, as shown in the 2006 US outbreak, and that RT-PCR and culture are the best current tests for vaccinated people.

sections.extract: Diagnostic challenges Laboratory diagnosis of mumps in highly-vaccinated populations is challenging, and new laboratory tools and diagnostic approaches are needed to accurately identify cases and better understand the epidemiology of mumps in highly-vaccinated populations. sections.title: Vaccine efficacy

summary.text: Reports prelicensure studies showing a single dose of Jeryl Lynn mumps vaccine was about 95% effective over short follow-up, and high efficacy for Leningrad-3 strain vaccines.

sections.extract: Vaccine efficacy Prelicensure studies conducted in over 7000 children enrolled in nursery or elementary schools found a single dose of mumps vaccines containing the Jeryl Lynn strain to be approximately 95% effective in preventing mumps disease (Hilleman et al., 1967; Weibel et al., 1967; Sugg et al., 1968). However, duration of follow-up was short (up to 20 months). In a smaller study, with 193 children exposed to

sections.title: Vaccine effectiveness

summary.text: Reviews postlicensure vaccine effectiveness from outbreak studies, with a median of 79% for one dose of Jeryl Lynn vaccine and lower figures for the Urabe strain. It reports that the Rubini strain showed little or no effectiveness and is no longer available. Two-dose Jeryl Lynn effectiveness had a median of 88%, usually but not significantly higher than one dose. It calls for research linking protection to neutralizing antibody levels and on the role of heterologous mumps strains.
